title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Real estate portfolio management
audience: Owners of portfolio management businesses who set fees or plan monthly revenue, including solo managers.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a portfolio management business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of fee income that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level a management business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of fee income adds to profit. The figure helps set a fee basis, decide when to take on another portfolio and check whether a new channel for owners can pay for itself. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages behind it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of properties in a month. For a manager they include software subscriptions, insurance, phone, a workspace share, professional fees and loan repayments on equipment. Variable costs move with each property or transaction. They include payment and bank fees on rent processing, advertising for each vacancy, tenant screening checks and any subcontractor fees for a visit. Express variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period. ANZ defines fixed and variable costs, and warns that costs must be covered to avoid operating at a loss (ANZ, Setting the right price for your product or service, dated 21 February 2025, last modified 22 July 2025). Check the percentage across at least three months, because one unusual vacancy can mislead. Measure each variable cost from your own records.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. The quantity one minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin, the share of each dollar of fee income left to cover fixed costs. Xero describes the same method: the margin divided by the price gives the ratio, and break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by that ratio (Xero Australia, Break-even point formula, dated 23 July 2026). Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 12 per cent becomes 0.12, and the contribution margin becomes 0.88.

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write each input first, with its source and its period. Compute the contribution margin. Divide the monthly fixed costs by it. Then convert the result into a number of properties at your average monthly fee per property, and round up to whole properties, because a part property does not cover costs. Xero's own glossary example rounds up in the same way (Xero, Break-even point formula). Use the average fee actually charged, after discounts and agreed waivers. No fee benchmark was found in the research for this course, so the fee in this lesson is hypothetical.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of fee income and not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue and not profit. Then keep one reconciled figure, written with its inputs, and drop the others. A figure with no inputs cannot be checked, and a figure that cannot be checked should not set a fee.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of fee income for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average monthly fee per property to get the number of properties needed, rounded up.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: A solo manager (hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson and not a fee benchmark) has fixed costs of $4,000 a month, variable costs of 12 per cent of fee income for payment, screening and advertising costs, and an average monthly fee of $250 per property.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many properties must the business manage each month to break even, and what should it check before setting the fee basis?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.12, which is 0.88. Break-even revenue is $4,000 divided by 0.88, which is $4,545.45 a month. At $250 a property that is 18.18 properties, so the manager needs 19 properties to cover costs. Each property contributes $220 ($250 multiplied by 0.88) towards fixed costs. Before setting the fee basis, check that the 12 per cent includes every payment and screening cost, that the $4,000 is a monthly figure, and that $250 is the average fee actually collected after waivers and agreed discounts. The fee and the percentage are hypothetical and do not indicate what any owner should pay.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months, including payment and screening costs
Property fee records showing the fee actually charged

commonErrors.error: Mixing monthly and annual figures, such as an annual software licence entered as a monthly cost
commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of fee income
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by fee income for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from a plan without its inputs
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own inputs and record the source and date of each input before using the result.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant.

This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority. Letting and rent collection for reward can need a licence in some states, and the fee income in this calculation may depend on that licence. Check the rule for each state before taking on the work.

Money held for owners follows the trust rules for the state. The NSW trust rule read for this course covers short-term rental only, so long-term rules are not confirmed. Keep trust money out of the break-even inputs unless you have confirmed how it is treated.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a fee.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs. Do not copy another plan's break-even figure.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost
Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $4,000 a month and variable costs are 12% of fee income. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same portfolio business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the owner today
Skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel

sourceReferences: Xero Australia, 'Break-even point formula' glossary entry, https://www.xero.com/au/glossary/break-even-point-formula/, dated 23 July 2026. Supports: contribution margin is price minus variable cost; break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio; job counts are rounded up to whole jobs. The glossary's own product examples are not used.

ANZ, 'Setting the right price for your product or service', https://www.anz.com.au/business/business-hub/starting-business/start/setting-the-right-price-for-your-product-or-service/, dated 21 February 2025, last modified 22 July 2025. Supports: definitions of fixed and variable costs, and the warning that costs must be covered to avoid operating at a loss.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: include total overheads in the price check.

NSW Fair Trading, 'Property management', https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/property-professionals/property-management, published 19 June 2025, modified 6 October 2026. Covers short-term rental only; long-term trust rules not confirmed.
Hypothetical figures ($4,000 fixed, 12 per cent variable, $250 fee per property) are invented for this lesson and are not market data, fee benchmarks or advice on what to charge.
